title: British politics
subtitle: lobby, petition, legislation, select committee
summary: Understand and use the vocabulary of the British political system - lobbying and petitioning, bills and legislation, select committees, constituents and the Speaker.

lesson.heading: Having your say
lesson.text: Ordinary citizens in the UK can **lobby** MPs and Members of the House of Lords (known as **peers**) about an issue - that is, try to influence their opinions. They can also **petition** the House of Commons: a formal process of sending a written appeal to an MP in a set format, which the MP then presents to the Commons.

examples.text: Citizens can **lobby** MPs and **peers** about a particular issue.
They can **petition** the House of Commons to request action.
Methods of **lobbying** range from sending letters to organising **rallies**.

lesson.note: Rallies are large political meetings or demonstrations.

lesson.heading: Bills and legislation
lesson.text: **Legislation** means possible future laws. A **Public Bill** is a proposal for a law currently under discussion. The **committee stage** is the period after a proposed law has been discussed by Parliament, when it is looked at in detail by a group of people.

examples.text: The public can comment on **legislation** going through Parliament.
The bill has had two readings in the House of Commons and is now going through the **committee stage**.
A **Select Committee** inquiry may **scrutinise** the work and policies of the government.
examples.note: to scrutinise = to look very closely at

lesson.heading: Who decides in the end
lesson.text: Lobbying often seeks to get the MP or peer to vote a certain way. However, this decision is **ultimately** - in the end - **down to** the MP's or peer's own **judgement**, and to the influence that existing **party policy** has on them. To be down to someone is to be their responsibility.

examples.text: The decision is **ultimately down to** the MP's own **judgement**.
On this particular issue, it is **down to** the individual MP how he or she votes.
I am not quite sure what **party policy** is on renewable energy.
Ministers have to read a lot of **briefing material** provided by their advisers.

lesson.heading: How petitions work
lesson.text: A petition must be properly **set out** - in the correct format - and carry at least one signature and address. Its text is published in **Hansard**, the official record of parliamentary business. MPs generally **present** all petitions they receive from their **constituents**, the people in their **constituency**, or political region.

examples.text: A petition to Parliament has to be **set out** in accordance with strict rules.
You can read **Hansard** to find out what has been happening in Parliament.
MPs will **present** all petitions they receive from their **constituents**.
It can also be created and submitted online, as an **e-petition**.

lesson.heading: The Speaker and the chamber
lesson.text: The **Speaker** is the MP with responsibility for controlling the way parliamentary business is done. MPs present petitions either by making a short statement in the **debating chamber** or by placing the petition in the Petition Bag behind the **Speaker's chair**. Government departments offer **observations** - comments - on all **substantive**, that is significant, petitions.

examples.text: MPs discuss proposed legislation in the **debating chamber** of the House of Commons.
The **Speaker's chair** is situated between the two sets of benches.
Departments are expected to offer **observations** on all **substantive** petitions.

lesson.heading: Select Committee vocabulary
rows: deal with more than one department
closely examine the consequences of decisions
complaints that have not been proven
follow closely to see how a job is done
a high level of knowledge covering many subjects
the full set of laws of a country

lesson.heading: Commons and Lords committees
lesson.text: There is a Commons Select Committee for each government department, examining spending, **policies** and administration. Lords Select Committees do not **shadow** government departments; they investigate specialist subjects, using the **wide-ranging expertise** of the Lords and the greater amount of time available to them.

examples.text: It is the role of the Health Select Committee to **shadow** the work done in the Department of Health.
There is a lot of **expertise** in the House of Lords because of the different professional backgrounds of its members.
The work of this committee is complex because it **crosses** departmental boundaries.

lesson.text: Lobby and petition are both verbs here: you lobby an MP and you petition the House of Commons.

exercises.prompt: Match the words to make political collocations.
MPs discuss proposed legislation in the ___ of the House of Commons.
exercises.explanation: The debating chamber is where parliamentary debates take place.

exercises.prompt: Before Question Time, Ministers have to read a lot of ___ provided by their advisers.
exercises.explanation: Briefing material is informational material prepared for someone before a meeting.

exercises.prompt: The bill has had two readings in the House of Commons and is now going through the ___.
exercises.hint: (when a group looks at it in detail)
exercises.explanation: At the committee stage a proposed law is looked at in detail by a group of people.

exercises.prompt: The ___ of individual MPs may be investigated if it is thought they have not behaved honestly.
exercises.explanation: Conduct is the formal word for behaviour.

exercises.prompt: There have been a number of ___ claiming that the Speaker is not doing his or her job properly.
exercises.explanation: Allegations are complaints that have not been proven.

exercises.prompt: A petition to Parliament has to be ___ out in accordance with strict rules.
exercises.explanation: To set out a document is to put it into the correct format.

exercises.prompt: It is the role of the Health Select Committee to ___ the work done in the Department of Health.
exercises.hint: (follow closely to see how a job is done)
exercises.explanation: Commons Select Committees shadow the work of government departments.

exercises.prompt: There is a lot of ___ in the House of Lords because of the very different professional backgrounds among its members.
exercises.explanation: Lords committees take advantage of the wide-ranging expertise of their members.

exercises.prompt: What does it mean to lobby an MP?
options: to try to influence their opinion on an issue
to send a formal written appeal in a set format
to vote against them at an election
to publish their speeches in Hansard
exercises.explanation: Lobbying is trying to influence the opinions of MPs and peers; a formal written appeal is a petition.

options: the people in the political region that elected them
the other members of their party
the members of the House of Lords
the civil servants in their department
exercises.explanation: Constituents are the people in an MP's constituency - the political region they represent.

exercises.statement: A lobbied MP has to do what his or her constituents request.
exercises.explanation: False - the decision is ultimately down to the MP to make up his or her own mind.

exercises.statement: You can read Hansard to find out what has been happening in Parliament.
exercises.explanation: Correct - Hansard is the official record of parliamentary business.

exercises.statement: Select Committees do not look at how individual MPs behave.
exercises.explanation: False - some Commons Committees do investigate allegations about the conduct of individual MPs.

exercises.prompt: Does each item belong to influencing Parliament, or to the work of committees?
Put this sentence about an MP's vote in order.
exercises.answer: The decision is ultimately down to the MP's own judgement
exercises.explanation: To be down to someone is to be their responsibility; ultimately means in the end.
